Neonates of the Armenian lizard emerge from their parchment-shelled eggs after an incubation period that depends on local thermal conditions, a common pattern across lacertid reptiles. At the moment of hatching, these young-of-year reptiles typically measure approximately 2.25 centimeters [Lb = approximately 2.25 centimeters] in snout-vent length, a figure that aligns closely with values reported for the congeneric Darevskia derjugini. This modest size at emergence reflects the energetic constraints of yolk-dependent development within a cleidoic egg. The hatchlings immediately begin a period of rapid mass gain as they transition to exogenous feeding, relying on small arthropod prey available in their rocky montane habitats. Their relatively small body size at this stage, compared to some other oviparous reptiles, may influence early-life survivorship and predation risk. Field observations suggest that the timing of eclosion is synchronized with seasonal peaks in prey abundance, allowing the endotrophic larvae to quickly replenish energy stores. The initial wet body mass of these hatchlings, based on measurements from closely related species, is believed to be around 0.26 grams [Wwb = around 0.26 grams], though direct data for Darevskia armeniaca remain limited.

As females grow and approach reproductive maturity, their body size increases substantially from the dimensions recorded at hatching. The attainment of this maximum body dimension is accompanied by a corresponding increase in body mass; sexually mature adult females achieve a peak wet weight of 9.57 grams [Wwi = 9.57 grams]. This substantial increase from the neonatal mass of roughly a quarter of a gram highlights the considerable investment in structural growth that occurs during the juvenile period. In comparative terms, the ultimate mass of this species is consistent with that of other rock lizards inhabiting similar temperate montane environments. The relationship between body size and fecundity is a central theme in the life history of this oviparous lacertid, as larger females typically produce more offspring.

The timing of oviposition is critical, as the incubating eggs must develop within a narrow window of favorable summer temperatures. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 20 °C [T = 20 °C], the maximum recorded longevity for this species reaches approximately 2920 days [am = approximately 2920 days], a duration equivalent to roughly eight years. The extended period of somatic growth and delayed reproduction contribute to this pattern, as individuals invest heavily in reaching a body size sufficient to support viable clutch production. In natural populations, senescence and age-related mortality likely occur at somewhat younger ages due to predation pressure and environmental stochasticity. Nonetheless, the potential for a multi-year reproductive life span allows females to compensate for their modest annual fecundity by breeding over several consecutive seasons. During this pre-reproductive interval, growing juveniles must navigate the risks of predation while maximizing food intake to fuel both maintenance and growth. The age at first reproduction in Darevskia armeniaca is comparable to that of several other Darevskia species inhabiting similar high-elevation refugia in the Caucasus region. This strategy of delayed but sustained reproduction over a relatively long life span contrasts with the faster pace of life observed in many lowland lacertids, where earlier maturation and shorter lifespans are more common evolutionary solutions to different ecological pressures.
